items.basis: The proposed vibration mechanism is unlikely to prevent particle settling and early deposit consolidation in nozzle inlets, as the 200 Hz frequency is too low to effectively counteract the settling forces acting on the particles. In industrial hoppers and chutes, the vibration frequencies used are typically much higher (e.g., 10-20 Hz) to achieve the desired effect.

The boundary condition of thermal-crown variation must stay inside 12 microns is unlikely to be met, as the vibration-induced stress on the header and nozzles may lead to increased thermal expansion and contraction, resulting in larger thermal-crown variations.

There is no evidence provided to support the claim that vibration-assisted transport is proven in industrial hoppers and chutes, and that deposits never consolidate if the surface never rests. In fact, most industrial applications of vibration-assisted transport involve much higher vibration frequencies and amplitudes than those proposed in this candidate.

The predicted effect of eliminating deposit consolidation in nozzle inlets and reducing clogging events per campaign is unlikely to be achieved, as the baseline system is already optimized for spray uniformity and thermal-crown control. The proposed vibration mechanism is unlikely to provide a significant improvement over the existing system.

The proposed implementation of two 200 Hz electro-mechanical shakers mounted on the header ends, with a 12 kW continuous drive, is unlikely to be feasible due to the high power requirements and the potential for vibration-induced stress on the header and nozzles.

The testable prediction of a bench header section vibrated at 200 Hz versus static showing no deposit consolidation after a 120-hour slurry exposure is ambiguous, as it does not account for the potential effects of vibration-induced stress on the header and nozzles, which may lead to increased thermal expansion and contraction.
